title: Pocket Money Tracker
pitch: Save up for the thing you really want.

words.intro: Pick something you really want. Track your money in and out, draw a **chart**, and let Python predict the exact week you can buy it.
words.finished: You built a real money planner. Show it to the grown-ups!
words.tinker: Keep tinkering: what if you saved 20 more every week? Change the weekly list and watch the finish week move.

milestones.title: Set a goal
milestones.goal: A savings goal that's really yours.

steps.instruction: Look at the last line: `goal - saved`. What will it print?
steps.explain: Without quotes, `goal - saved` is maths: Python opens both boxes and works out 800 - 150 = **650**.
hints: Look at `goal - saved` in the last print.
Variables without quotes are boxes. Python uses what's inside them.
If `a = 10` and `b = 3`, then `print(a - b)` prints 7.
I still need 650. Pick that and Run.

steps.instruction: What do **you** want to save for? Change `goal_item` to your thing and `goal` to its price in rupees (a number, no quotes).
hints: Change the first two lines.
Words need quotes. Numbers don't.
`goal_item = "football"` and `goal = 1200`.
`goal_item = "______"` and `goal = ____`
`goal_item = "skateboard"` and `goal = 2500`. Use your own if you like!

milestones.title: Track money in and out
milestones.goal: Lists of money in and money out, added up.

steps.instruction: Money comes in and goes out, so it lives in two **lists**. What will "Saved so far" show?
steps.explain: `sum(money_in)` is 100 + 50 + 200 + 50 = 400. `sum(money_out)` is 30 + 20 = 50. So 400 - 50 = **350**. `len(money_in)` counts the amounts: 4 weeks.
hints: Look at the line `saved = sum(money_in) - sum(money_out)`.
`sum(list)` adds up every number in a list.
350. Pick that and Run.

steps.instruction: Log more money! Add **2 more** amounts to the end of `money_in` (pocket money, a birthday gift…) and **1 more** thing you spent to `money_out`.
hints: Add numbers inside the square brackets, at the end.
Put a comma before each new number. No quotes for numbers.
`[100, 50]` with one more becomes `[100, 50, 75]`.

milestones.title: Chart it
milestones.goal: A bar chart that climbs towards your goal.

steps.instruction: This code adds your savings up week by week into a list called `totals`. Fill the blank so the chart shows **totals**, and watch the bars climb to your goal.
hints: The blank is the first thing inside `stage.bar_chart(...)`.
`bar_chart` draws one bar per number in the list you give it.
`stage.bar_chart([10, 30, 60], ["a", "b", "c"])` draws three growing bars.
`stage.bar_chart(t_____, labels, ...)`
`stage.bar_chart(totals, labels, goal=goal, title="Saving for my " + goal_item)`.

steps.instruction: Quick check: with `weekly = [100, 50, 200, 50, 80, 120]`, what does `totals` hold after the loop?
steps.explain: Each time round, `running` grows by that week's amount, and `.append()` adds the new running total to the list. So each total includes every week before it.
hints: Look at the printed line that starts with Totals.
`running = running + amount` keeps a running total.
After week 1: 100. After week 2: 100 + 50 = 150.
Then 150 + 200 = 350, and so on.

milestones.title: Predict the finish week
milestones.goal: Python tells you the exact week you can buy it.

steps.instruction: Now Python looks into the future: it keeps adding a week of savings **while** the total is still below the goal. Fill the blank with the right comparison.

check.description: Now you know the exact week!

hints: The blank is in `while total ___ goal:`.
The loop should keep going as long as you haven't reached the goal yet.
`<` means less than. `>` means greater than.
`while total _ goal:`
`while total < goal:`. Run it to see your finish week.

steps.instruction: Make it your plan: change the numbers in `weekly` to what you could really save. Could you reach your goal sooner? (If you add weeks, add labels like `"W7"` too.)

check.description: That's a real plan. Show a grown-up!

hints: Change the numbers in the `weekly = [...]` list.
Bigger weekly numbers mean an earlier finish week.
`weekly = [120, 120, 150, 100, 200, 120]`. Run it and see the week change.
